claims.text: The Co-free FeNiCrMn alloy is derived from equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi.
The as-solidified Co-free FeNiCrMn alloy is a single-phase solid solution.
A temperature- and strain-rate-dependent transition in dislocation dynamics governs the alloy's dynamic strength–ductility balance.
The absence of Co produces substantial local lattice distortion.
Removing Co increases lattice distortion relative to equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi.
Increased lattice distortion raises local friction-stress barriers to dislocation motion.
At low temperatures and/or high strain rates, restricted dislocation glide dominates deformation.
Glide-dominated deformation at low temperature or high strain rate produces high strength.
Glide-dominated deformation at low temperature or high strain rate limits ductility.
At elevated temperatures and/or lower strain rates, thermal activation overcomes local barriers and increases cross-slip.
Increased cross-slip facilitates more uniform plastic deformation.
More uniform plastic deformation caused by cross-slip increases ductility.
Higher temperature and/or lower strain rate moderately reduces strength relative to low-temperature/high-rate deformation.
Equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi has less pronounced lattice-distortion effects than Co-free FeNiCrMn.
At high temperatures and low strain rates, the Co-free alloy will exhibit more cross-slip activity than equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi.
At high temperatures and low strain rates, the Co-free alloy will exhibit greater ductility than equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi.
The proposed mechanism applies from approximately 77 K to 800 K and from 10^-4 s^-1 to 10^-1 s^-1.
The proposed mechanism may cease to apply in regimes where phase transformations or twinning govern deformation.
Changes in stacking-fault energy may also influence the dynamic response.

contradictions.description: The stated baseline is CoCrFeMnNi at room temperature and low strain rate, whereas the strength prediction is referenced to the Co-free alloy's low-temperature/high-rate performance and the falsification experiment also invokes matched comparisons across the full test range. These are different comparison baselines, making the intended relative prediction internally inconsistent.
